question.problem:
The function $f(x)$ is defined for every real number $x$ and is given by

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}(c-x)^{2}+3c, & x\ne -1, \\ -5, & x=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-1$, what are the possible values of $c?$
question.worked_solution:
From the definition of $f(x),$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -1}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to -1}((c-x)^{2}+3c) \\  & =(c-(-1))^{2}+3c \\  & ={c}^{2}+2c+1+3c \\  & ={c}^{2}+5c+1.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=-1,$ we must have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -1}f(x) & =f(-1) \\ {c}^{2}+5c+1 & =-5 \\ {c}^{2}+5c+6 & =0 \\ (c+2)(c+3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, $c=-2$ or $c=-3.$
